# System Tour: From SQL to Native Code {#sec-system-tour}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
:::

This chapter is a whirlwind tour. By the end of it you should have a
mental picture of every module in the engine, in the right order, and
know roughly which chapter to turn to for each. We will not stop to
explain anything in detail. We are racing through the pipeline from
SQL text to running native code, in about thirty pages, using a
single demo query as our chaperone.

The query is the smallest one we can write that exercises the whole
stack. It comes from the README:

```sql
CREATE LOGICAL SOURCE demo(value UINT64);
CREATE PHYSICAL SOURCE FOR demo
    TYPE File
    SET('./demo-input.csv' AS `SOURCE`.FILE_PATH,
        'CSV' AS PARSER.`TYPE`,
        '\n' AS PARSER.TUPLE_DELIMITER,
        ',' AS PARSER.FIELD_DELIMITER);
CREATE SINK result(demo.value UINT64)
    TYPE File
    SET('./demo-output.csv' AS `SINK`.FILE_PATH,
        'CSV' AS `SINK`.OUTPUT_FORMAT);
SELECT value FROM demo INTO result;
```

Three DDL statements declare a source, a physical implementation of
that source, and a sink. The fourth statement is the actual query: a
trivial projection that copies tuples from `demo` into `result`. It
has no filter, no join, no window. Anything more complicated would
double the length of this chapter without changing the structure of
the tour.

We follow that query through seven stages.

![The seven stages a query passes through, from text to running tasks. Each arrow corresponds to one chapter later in the book.](../figures/tikz/ch02-pipeline.svg){#fig-pipeline width=100%}

Each arrow is one chapter later in the book. Here we will spend
about three pages per stage, name the key class and file, and move
on.

---

## 2.1 Stage 1: SQL → AST → bound logical plan {#sec-stage1-parse}

The text of the query enters the engine through `nes-sql-parser/`,
an ANTLR4-based parser. The grammar lives in
`nes-sql-parser/AntlrSQL.g4` (about 600 lines). The grammar covers
the four DDL/DML shapes we need:

- `CREATE LOGICAL SOURCE` — defines a schema by name.
- `CREATE PHYSICAL SOURCE` — binds an implementation (file, TCP,
  generator) to a logical source.
- `CREATE SINK` — defines a sink schema and implementation.
- `SELECT … INTO` — the query proper.

The parser does the syntactic work; it produces an ANTLR parse tree.
A second component called the *binder* converts that tree into a
typed `LogicalPlan`. The binder lives in
`nes-sql-parser/src/StatementBinder.cpp`. Binding is where the engine
checks that names resolve, that types make sense, and that the
schemas of sources and sinks match the projections in the query. The
output of the binder is a `LogicalPlan` — a typed, validated DAG of
operators.

A `LogicalPlan` is defined in
`nes-logical-operators/include/Plans/LogicalPlan.hpp`. Its core is a
vector of root operators and a query identifier:

```cpp
// nes-logical-operators/include/Plans/LogicalPlan.hpp
class LogicalPlan {
public:
    explicit LogicalPlan(LogicalOperator rootOperator);
    explicit LogicalPlan(QueryId queryId,
                         std::vector<LogicalOperator> rootOperators);
    [[nodiscard]] QueryId getQueryId() const;
    [[nodiscard]] std::vector<LogicalOperator> getRootOperators() const;
    [[nodiscard]] LogicalPlan withRootOperators(
        const std::vector<LogicalOperator>& operators) const;
};
```

For our demo query the binder produces a plan with one root: an
`InlineSinkLogicalOperator` named `result`, whose child is a
`SourceDescriptorLogicalOperator` named `demo`. A projection node sits
between them, but for `SELECT value FROM demo INTO result` the
projection is the identity, so the optimiser will eliminate it
shortly.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.1: the post-bind plan, in text"}
The bound plan can be visualised as:

```
SinkLogicalOperator(name=result, schema={demo$value: UINT64})
└── SourceDescriptorLogicalOperator(name=demo, schema={demo$value: UINT64})
```

Two operators, one parent-child edge. Note the `demo$value`
qualified name: NebulaStream uses `$` to separate the source
qualifier from the field name. We will see this convention again
in Chapter 6.
:::

Chapter 5 covers this stage in full.

---

## 2.2 Stage 2: bound plan → optimised plan {#sec-stage2-optimise}

The bound logical plan goes into the query optimiser, which lives in
`nes-query-optimizer/`. The entry point is `QueryOptimizer::optimize`,
defined in `nes-query-optimizer/src/QueryOptimizer.cpp`. The
optimiser is a sequence of pure-function rules:

```cpp
// nes-query-optimizer/src/QueryOptimizer.cpp
LogicalPlan QueryOptimizer::optimize(
    const LogicalPlan& plan,
    const QueryOptimizerConfiguration& defaultQueryOptimization)
{
    DecideJoinTypesRule joinTypeDecider(defaultQueryOptimization.joinStrategy);
    DecideMemoryLayoutRule memoryLayoutDecider;
    constexpr RedundantUnionRemovalRule redundantUnionRemovalRule{};
    constexpr RedundantProjectionRemovalRule redundantProjectionRemovalRule{};
    constexpr TypeInferenceRule typeInferenceRule{};

    auto optimizedPlan = LogicalPlan{plan};
    redundantProjectionRemovalRule.apply(optimizedPlan);
    redundantUnionRemovalRule.apply(optimizedPlan);
    typeInferenceRule.apply(optimizedPlan);
    optimizedPlan = joinTypeDecider.apply(optimizedPlan);
    optimizedPlan = memoryLayoutDecider.apply(optimizedPlan);
    return optimizedPlan;
}
```

Five rules, applied in sequence. For our demo query:

- `RedundantProjectionRemoval` deletes the identity projection.
- `RedundantUnionRemoval` does nothing (no unions).
- `TypeInference` annotates every operator with its input and output
  schemas.
- `DecideJoinTypes` does nothing (no joins).
- `DecideMemoryLayout` chooses row vs. columnar — currently always
  row, with the columnar path stubbed for future work (Chapter 4).

The optimiser is unusually small for a database engine. There is no
cost-based optimisation, no plan-space exploration, no statistics.
Every rule is a syntactic transformation. The reasoning is
pragmatic: streaming queries are typically short and shallow, and the
cost of a wrong plan is amortised over the query's lifetime, not
incurred on each request. We will discuss this trade-off in
Chapter 9.

---

## 2.3 Stage 3: logical → physical {#sec-stage3-lower}

The optimised logical plan is "what to compute." The physical plan is
"how to compute it." The conversion happens in
`nes-query-compiler/`, specifically the `LowerToPhysicalOperators`
phase. For our demo query, the lowering chooses:

- The source operator becomes a `SourcePhysicalOperator` that produces
  `TupleBuffer`s by calling into the `FileSource` implementation.
- The sink becomes a `SinkPhysicalOperator` that consumes
  `TupleBuffer`s and forwards them to the `FileSink` implementation
  (which uses a `CSVOutputFormatter`).

The base of the physical operator hierarchy is
`nes-physical-operators/include/PhysicalOperator.hpp`. Like its
logical counterpart, it is a C++20 concept rather than a virtual
class. Every physical operator implements `setup`, `open`, `close`
and `execute` — the lifecycle methods called during code generation.

::: {.callout-tip title="Real-system reference: how this maps to Flink"}
Flink also has a logical and physical plan, with similar lowering.
The visible difference is that Flink's physical plan is the input
to a Janino-compiled per-operator Java class; NebulaStream's
physical plan is the input to a tracing JIT. Functionally similar;
mechanically very different. Chapter 12 covers this gap in detail.
:::

The physical plan for our demo query has two operators with one
edge between them. We will look at the physical operator hierarchy
in detail in Chapter 10.

---

## 2.4 Stage 4: physical plan → pipelined plan {#sec-stage4-pipeline}

A physical plan is a DAG of operators. A pipelined plan is a DAG of
*pipelines*, where each pipeline is a chain of operators that can be
fused into a single tight loop and a single chunk of generated
code. Pipeline boundaries occur at operators that cannot be fused
through — *pipeline breakers* — most commonly stateful operators like
hash-join builds, aggregations, and window triggers.

The phase that does this is `PipeliningPhase`, defined in
`nes-query-compiler/private/Phases/PipeliningPhase.hpp`. For our
demo query — `Source → Sink` with no breaker between them — the
result is a single pipeline containing both operators.

```
Pipeline 1: [SourcePhysicalOperator(demo) → SinkPhysicalOperator(result)]
```

A more interesting query — say `SELECT count(*) FROM demo GROUP BY
key` — would produce two pipelines: one ending at the aggregation
build, and one starting at the aggregation probe. We will see the
multi-pipeline case in Chapter 11.

---

## 2.5 Stage 5: pipelined plan → compiled plan {#sec-stage5-compile}

The pipelined plan now goes to the JIT. The phase is
`LowerToCompiledQueryPlanPhase`, in
`nes-query-compiler/private/Phases/LowerToCompiledQueryPlanPhase.hpp`.
This is the most complex phase in the engine, and Chapter 12 spends
its entire length on it. The summary version: each pipeline becomes
an `ExecutablePipelineStage` produced by tracing through Nautilus,
which records the pipeline's operations as a sequence of operations
on `nautilus::val<>` typed values. The resulting trace is lowered
through MLIR to LLVM IR and JIT-compiled into a function pointer.

The single configuration option that matters here is the execution
mode:

```cpp
// nes-query-compiler/private/Phases/LowerToCompiledQueryPlanPhase.cpp
nautilus::engine::Options options;
options.setOption("mlir.enableMultithreading", false);
switch (pipelineQueryPlan->getExecutionMode())
{
    case ExecutionMode::COMPILER:
        options.setOption("engine.Compilation", true);
        break;
    case ExecutionMode::INTERPRETER:
        options.setOption("engine.Compilation", false);
        break;
}
```

Two modes. `COMPILER` produces native code, the default. `INTERPRETER`
runs the trace as an interpreter, which is much slower but
incomparably easier to debug — it is the mode you flip to when a
generated function gives you a wrong answer and you want to see why.
We will use `INTERPRETER` extensively in this book's reading
exercises.

The output of this phase is a `CompiledQueryPlan`, defined in
`nes-executable/include/CompiledQueryPlan.hpp`. It contains the
compiled `ExecutablePipelineStage`s plus fully-resolved
`SourceDescriptor`s and `SinkDescriptor`s — everything the worker
needs to execute, with no further coordinator round-trip.

---

## 2.6 Stage 6: compiled plan → running query {#sec-stage6-run}

The `CompiledQueryPlan` is registered with the query engine
(`nes-query-engine/`). Registration causes:

1. The engine constructs an `ExecutableQueryPlan` from the
   `CompiledQueryPlan`. This adds runtime state — counters, callbacks,
   per-pipeline operator handlers.
2. The engine wraps each pipeline in a `RunningQueryPlanNode`
   (defined in `nes-query-engine/RunningQueryPlan.hpp`), which holds
   a reference count of in-flight `WorkTask`s and a `weak_ptr` for
   safe cross-thread reference.
3. Sources are wrapped in `RunningSource` instances (also in
   `nes-query-engine/`) and started.

Once running, the engine uses the two-queue scheduler we examined
exhaustively in Chapter 15. To recap: sources push `TupleBuffer`s
into the bounded admission queue as `WorkTask`s; worker threads pull
from a logical merge of an unbounded internal queue (preferred) and
the admission queue (fallback); compiled pipeline functions process
buffers and emit follow-up `WorkTask`s into the unbounded internal
queue.

For our demo query, the file source reads `demo-input.csv`, the
`CSVInputFormatter` parses lines into `TupleBuffer`s, the compiled
pipeline projects (in this case, copies) the `value` field, and the
sink's `CSVOutputFormatter` writes the values to `demo-output.csv`.
End to end, in production execution mode, this is approximately one
function call per tuple, plus the I/O. The compiled code path has
the same overhead profile as a hand-written loop with a switch.

## 2.7 Putting the modules in order {#sec-modules-overview}

Twenty-three `nes-*` modules on `origin/main`, in roughly the
order they participate in a query's life:

| Module | Purpose | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| `nes-common` | Identifiers, logging, error macros, exception list | 17 |
| `nes-configurations` | Engine configuration types | 18 |
| `nes-data-types` | Schemas, types, fields | 3 |
| `nes-memory` | TupleBuffer, BufferManager | 3, 4 |
| `nes-runtime` | Shared runtime utilities | (cross-cutting) |
| `nes-executable` | `CompiledQueryPlan` and ExecutablePipelineStage | 11, 14 |
| `nes-sql-parser` | ANTLR4 grammar, statement binding | 5 |
| `nes-logical-operators` | Logical operator algebra | 6 |
| `nes-sources` | Source descriptors and registry | 8 |
| `nes-sinks` | Sink descriptors and registry | 8 |
| `nes-input-formatters` | Raw bytes → TupleBuffer | 8 |
| `nes-output-formatters` | TupleBuffer → raw bytes | 8 |
| `nes-query-optimizer` | Rule-based logical optimisation | 9, 10 |
| `nes-physical-operators` | Physical operator implementations | 10 |
| `nes-query-compiler` | Pipelining, lowering to executable | 11 |
| `nes-nautilus` | JIT, MLIR backend, runtime data structures | 12 |
| `nes-plugins` | Optional source/sink/operator plugins | 13 |
| `nes-query-engine` | Task scheduling, runtime, lifecycle | 14, 15 |
| `nes-distributed` | Distributed plan, worker catalog, network topology | 19 |
| `nes-network` | Rust+C++ FFI inter-worker channels | 19 |
| `nes-single-node-worker` | Worker process, gRPC service | 18 |
| `nes-frontend` | REPL and CLI clients | 18 |
| `nes-systests` | System-level `.test` file suite | 20 |

Earlier drafts of this book listed 16 modules. That count was
correct for the pinned commit at the time of writing
(`cd3ef68c73`, a feature branch) but has been wrong on
`origin/main` since the distribution layer landed. The two new
distribution modules (`nes-distributed`, `nes-network`) are the
subject of Chapter 19. The other modules previously listed under
"three more directories" — `nes-frontend`, `nes-systests` — are
now top-level entries. `nes-runtime`, `nes-configurations`, and
`nes-executable` were always present but were under-described.

Two non-`nes-*` directories complete the picture:

- `grpc/` contains the protobuf service definitions used by
  the worker (Chapter 18).
- `cmake/` contains the build helpers, including the plugin
  registry generator (Chapter 13).

## 2.8 What we glossed over {#sec-glossed-over}

We compressed thirty-five pages of careful explanation into one
chapter. Most of the compression was honest summarisation. Some of
it was outright omission. For the record:

- The watermark machinery and the four progress identifiers
  (`OriginId`, `SequenceNumber`, `ChunkNumber`, `Watermark`) do not
  appear in our demo query at all because there is no window. They
  appear in essentially every other query. Chapter 7 is dedicated to
  them.
- We described JIT compilation in a paragraph. It is the single most
  consequential design choice in the engine, and Chapter 12 spends
  its entire length on the tracing approach Nautilus uses.
- We did not mention error handling. Every stage above can fail.
  Chapter 17 covers the ~80 named exception types that NebulaStream
  defines and how `INVARIANT`/`PRECONDITION` macros work alongside
  them.
- We did not mention deployment. The whole tour assumed a single-node
  worker, because that is what NebulaStream currently fully
  implements. Chapter 19 is honest about what is and is not yet
  distributed.

If you read this chapter and found a stage opaque, the corresponding
chapter is the cure. If you read this chapter and found nothing
opaque, you should probably be reviewing the engine, not reading
this book.

---

## Summary {#sec-ch2-summary}

A NebulaStream query passes through seven stages: parse, bind,
optimise, lower, pipeline, compile, run. Each stage is one or two
modules. Each transformation is a pure function, except the last,
which spawns running threads. The total time from `nes-repl` accepting
the SQL to the first tuple landing in the sink is, for a small
query, on the order of milliseconds — most of it spent in the JIT.

The remaining 21 chapters elaborate one stage at a time. By the end
of Part IV (Chapter 18), you will have visited every line of code
this chapter waved at, in roughly twenty times the depth.

---

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch2-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 2.1: trace the demo query"}
Build NebulaStream and submit the demo query from this chapter
verbatim. Watch the worker log at TRACE level:

```shell
./cmake-build-debug/nes-single-node-worker/nes-single-node-worker \
    --logging.level=TRACE
```

In another terminal, submit the demo query through `nes-repl`. The
worker log will show the seven stages in order. Identify the lines
that mark the boundary between each stage. Some are easy to spot
(the parser logs the SQL); some are subtle (the boundary between
optimiser and lowering is a single class instantiation).
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 2.2: compare execution modes"}
Run a join systest in `INTERPRETER` mode and compare its wall-clock
time to the same systest in `COMPILER` mode (the default). Choose,
for example:

```shell
cmake-build-debug/systest/systest \
    -t nes-systests/operator/join/JoinMultipleStreams.test:1 \
    -- --worker.default_query_execution.execution_mode=COMPILER
cmake-build-debug/systest/systest \
    -t nes-systests/operator/join/JoinMultipleStreams.test:1 \
    -- --worker.default_query_execution.execution_mode=INTERPRETER
```

The interpreter is typically 10–100× slower. Where does the
overhead come from? Hint: the interpreter walks the same trace the
compiler emits, but executes each operation through a virtual
dispatch.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 2.3: count the touchpoints"}
For each of the seven stages, find one class whose name contains the
stage's verb (Parser, Binder, Optimizer, Lowering, Pipelining,
Compiler, Engine). Open each in your editor and read its top-level
header comment. Total time: 15 minutes; total reward: a much
sharper sense of where chapter boundaries fall.
:::
